c.tagline: A mountain town wedged between glacier-fed lakes and jagged Rocky Mountain peaks in Canada's first national park

card: Contactless and card payment (including tap-to-pay) are the norm virtually everywhere, from hotels to trailhead kiosks; cash is rarely needed.

taxi.color: no standard livery — mostly private sedans and vans
taxi.fareNote: Metered fares are standard in town; Roam Transit buses are a cheaper alternative to Lake Louise and Canmore

emergency.note: Parks Canada visitor safety staff and mountain rescue respond to backcountry and trail emergencies

english.label: Easy to get by in English

walk: Downtown Banff along Banff Avenue is compact and walkable, with the Bow Falls and Cave and Basin trails an easy stroll from the center; Lake Louise, Moraine Lake, and the Icefields Parkway require a car, shuttle, or Roam Transit bus.

safety.safety: Very safe; Banff is a well-managed national park town with low crime, comfortable for solo travelers at any hour
safety.crime: Petty theft (unattended valuables in parked cars, a known issue at trailhead parking lots) is the main risk; wildlife encounters (bears, elk) are the bigger practical safety consideration

hood_landmark.Banff Avenue / Downtown: Banff Avenue's shops, framed by Cascade Mountain at the end of the street
hood_landmark.Bow Falls / Surprise Corner: Bow Falls viewpoint and Fairmont Banff Springs
hood_landmark.Tunnel Mountain: Tunnel Mountain hoodoos and campground area

avoid.reason: Crime is minimal; the real hazards are wildlife — keep well clear of elk and carry bear spray on trails.

hood_desc: The compact commercial heart of Banff along Banff Avenue, lined with outdoor gear shops, restaurants and bars and running down to the Bow River bridge - the natural hub for most visitors, and where the Roam buses connect.
A short walk from downtown, home to the iconic Fairmont Banff Springs castle-hotel and the roaring Bow Falls viewpoint.
A small mountain hamlet about an hour from Banff townsite, built around the turquoise glacial lake and its historic grand hotel.
A residential and campground area on the edge of downtown, known for hoodoo rock formations and hiking trailheads.
lodging: HI Lake Louise Alpine Centre - Hostel

water.note: Tap water is safe and excellent quality.

transit.sys: Roam Transit public bus network connecting Banff, Lake Louise, and Canmore
transit.hours: Roughly 6am-11pm, seasonal reduced winter hours to Lake Louise
transit.pay: Contactless card, exact cash, or the Roam Transit app; day passes available
transit.map: Route maps at roamtransit.com and posted at stops
transit.note: Parking at Moraine Lake and Lake Louise fills quickly in summer — many visitors are required to use the shuttle system

transport.air: Calgary International Airport (YYC), about 130 km / 1.5 hours away, is the main gateway
transport.train: Rocky Mountaineer offers a scenic seasonal tourist rail service to Banff; no regular passenger rail
transport.bus: Banff Airporter and On-It Regional Transit connect Calgary Airport to Banff; Roam Transit covers local and Canmore routes
transport.ferry: None — Banff is inland in the Rocky Mountains with no ferry service
transport.car: Reachable via the Trans-Canada Highway (Hwy 1) from Calgary; a car (or the Icefields Parkway shuttle) is useful for reaching Lake Louise, Moraine Lake, and the Icefields Parkway

airport.name: Calgary International Airport
airport.transport: Banff Airporter shuttle bus (~CAD $70 one-way) or On-It Regional Transit; taxi/private transfer roughly CAD $250-300

net.m: Good 4G/5G coverage in Banff townsite and along the Trans-Canada Highway; signal drops in backcountry areas and along parts of the Icefields Parkway
net.w: Free wifi standard in hotels, cafes, and the Banff visitor center
net.fwn: Free wifi widely available in hotels and downtown cafes
net.ap: A Canadian prepaid SIM or eSIM (Rogers, Telus, Bell) is easy to buy at Calgary Airport

tip.s: 15-18% is standard for hotel staff, tour guides, and ski instructors
tip.r: 15-20% is customary at restaurants; often pre-suggested on the payment terminal

food.name: Alberta AAA beef steak
food.desc: Grain-finished Alberta beef, dry-aged and grilled over open flame. The province's signature product and the centrepiece of most Banff menus.

places.name: Chuck's Steakhouse
places.note: Whole-animal Alberta beef program with dry-aging room visible from the dining floor.

places.name: Saltlik Steakhouse
places.note: Long-running steakhouse known for its crust-seared certified Alberta beef cuts.

places.name: Sky Bistro
places.note: Gondola-top dining room serving Alberta beef with panoramic Bow Valley views.

food.name: Bison burger and short ribs
food.desc: Lean, slightly sweet prairie bison, served as a thick burger or slow-braised short ribs. A Rocky Mountain staple with First Nations roots.

places.name: The Bison Restaurant and Terrace
places.note: Braised bison short ribs and bison onion soup are the signature plates here.

places.name: Banff Ave Brewing Co.
places.note: Upstairs brewpub pairing its bison burger with beers brewed on site.

places.name: Eddie Burger Bar
places.note: Small, busy burger bar with bison and elk patties; book or expect a wait.

food.name: Elk
food.desc: Farmed Alberta elk served as steak, sausage or thin slices seared tableside on a hot rock. Deeper and gamier than beef, very lean.

places.name: The Grizzly House
places.note: Fondue institution since 1967; hot-rock game platters of elk, buffalo and venison.

places.name: Deer Lodge
places.note: Historic log lodge dining room with elk steaks and regional Alberta produce.

places.name: The Bison Restaurant and Terrace
places.note: Rotates elk onto its Rocky Mountain game menu alongside bison.

food.name: Poutine
food.desc: Fries, squeaky cheese curds and gravy, the Canadian classic; Banff kitchens load it with elk gravy, pulled bison or duck confit.

places.name: Eddie Burger Bar
places.note: Elk-gravy poutine that regularly tops local best-poutine lists.

places.name: Banff Ave Brewing Co.
places.note: Pub-scale poutine and other elevated bar food with mountain views from the balcony.

places.name: Sky Bistro
places.note: Duck poutine on the gourmet Canadian menu at the top of the gondola.

food.name: BeaverTails
food.desc: Hand-stretched fried dough shaped like a beaver's tail, dusted with cinnamon sugar or spread with chocolate hazelnut. A Canadian street sweet.

places.name: BeaverTails Banff Avenue
places.note: The busiest of the two town shops; lines run down the block on winter weekends.

places.name: BeaverTails Bear Street
places.note: Quieter second location; same classic cinnamon-sugar and chocolate versions.

food.name: Rocky Mountain trout and Arctic char
food.desc: Cold-water Canadian fish, usually pan-seared or cedar-planked, served with foraged mushrooms or berries. The non-red-meat local signature.

places.name: The Maple Leaf
places.note: Regional Canadian menu with char and trout plus a huge Canadian wine list.

places.name: Park Distillery Restaurant and Bar
places.note: Campfire-style cooking, rotisserie and trout, with spirits distilled on site.

places.name: Sky Bistro
places.note: Serves Arctic char alongside Alberta beef at 2,281 metres.

food.name: Rocky Mountain craft beer
food.desc: Beer brewed with glacier-fed mountain water; Banff and Canmore taprooms pour spruce-tip ales, lagers and IPAs made a few minutes from the trailheads.

places.name: Banff Ave Brewing Co.
places.note: Banff's own brewpub, brewing on site with a wide flight selection.

places.name: Three Bears Brewery and Restaurant
places.note: Glass-walled brewhouse in the middle of the restaurant; food menu to match.

places.name: Park Distillery Restaurant and Bar
places.note: Also pours local craft alongside its own grain-to-glass spirits.

food.name: Caesar cocktail
food.desc: Canada's national cocktail: vodka, clamato, hot sauce and celery salt over a spiced rim, garnished to excess. Best made with Alberta-distilled vodka.

places.name: Park Distillery Restaurant and Bar
places.note: Mixes Caesars with its own glacier-water vodka distilled in the building.

places.name: High Rollers
places.note: Bowling-alley bar with loaded Caesars, pizza and a long local beer list.

places.name: The Maple Leaf
places.note: Classic Canadian bar program pairing Caesars with regional small plates.

landmarks: Lake Louise
The Rockies' turquoise showpiece, framed by Victoria Glacier and the grand Fairmont chateau, glorious for canoeing in summer and skating in winter.
Moraine Lake
An impossibly blue glacial lake beneath the Valley of the Ten Peaks, the vista once printed on Canada's twenty-dollar bill.
Banff Gondola and Sulphur Mountain
An eight-minute gondola ride to a summit boardwalk with 360-degree panoramas over six mountain ranges and the Bow Valley.
Fairmont Banff Springs Hotel
The 'Castle in the Rockies,' a baronial 1888 railway hotel whose turrets rise from pine forest above Bow Falls.
Johnston Canyon
Catwalks bolted to limestone cliffs lead past churning waterfalls to the Ink Pots, jade-colored mineral springs in a mountain meadow.
Lake Minnewanka
Banff's largest lake, a glacial fjord-like reservoir offering scenic cruises, lakeside drives, and a submerged ghost town for divers.
Cave and Basin National Historic Site
The steamy thermal cave whose 1883 discovery by railway workers gave birth to Canada's entire national park system.
Bow Falls
A broad, thundering curtain of the Bow River just below the Banff Springs Hotel, reached by an easy riverside stroll from town.
Vermilion Lakes
A chain of tranquil wetland lakes minutes from downtown, the classic spot to photograph Mount Rundle mirrored at sunrise.
Banff Upper Hot Springs
Historic mineral-rich pools at 1,585 meters where bathers soak in steaming water while gazing at snow-dusted Mount Rundle.

train.note: Banff has no scheduled passenger rail - VIA Rail's transcontinental route runs through Jasper to the north, not through Banff. The only trains here are the seasonal luxury Rocky Mountaineer (https://www.rockymountaineer.com/) between Banff, Lake Louise and Vancouver, which is a multi-day holiday product rather than transport. Arrive by coach or car from Calgary.

bus.note: No international coaches. Banff Airporter (https://www.banffairporter.com/) and Brewster Express (https://www.banffjaspercollection.com/) run frequent shuttles from Calgary airport in about 2 hours, and Rider Express (https://riderexpress.ca/) and On-It seasonal buses connect Calgary and Lake Louise more cheaply. Roam Transit covers Banff townsite, Lake Louise and the Moraine Lake shuttle, which is compulsory in summer since private cars are barred from the Moraine Lake road.

ferry.note: Banff is high in the Rockies with no navigable water, so there are no ferries. Boat cruises on Lake Minnewanka and canoe rentals on the Bow are recreation rather than transport.

half.name: Yoho National Park
half.blurb: A British Columbia park across the Continental Divide from Banff, home to the turquoise Emerald Lake and the thundering Takakkaw Falls.

half.name: Kootenay National Park
half.blurb: A park south of Banff along Highway 93, with the hot mineral pools of Radium Hot Springs at its western end.

full.name: Columbia Icefield & Athabasca Glacier
full.blurb: A vast ice field straddling the Continental Divide along the Icefields Parkway, with a glacier walk onto the Athabasca Glacier's blue ice.
